feedback: If a learner measures from the surface instead of the normal, point out that the normal is the perpendicular drawn first at the contact point, and every angle is read from it — re-measure one case both ways to see the difference.

If a learner says the ray leaves the block without bending or bends toward the normal a second time: on exit the ray speeds up (glass/water→air) so it bends AWAY from the normal; for a parallel-sided block the emerging ray is parallel to the ray that went in. Trace the speed change at both boundaries.
If a learner expects the 0° ray to bend: it still changes speed, but with no angle there is no sideways lag, so it goes straight through — the bend needs an angled crossing, not just a denser medium.

To make the slow-side-lags idea physical, picture a line of marching-band members (or a car's pair of wheels) crossing at an angle onto slower ground: the side that reaches the slow medium first is held back, so the whole line swings toward the normal — the same angled speed difference bends the light ray.
If a learner draws a curved path inside the block: light travels in a straight line within each medium and changes direction abruptly only at the boundary (a kink, not a curve).

Confirm the virtual image by noting that no light actually reaches behind the mirror — the dashed rays only show where reflected light appears to come from; the image is upright, the same size, equal distance behind, and laterally inverted.
activities.intendedInsight: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection when both are measured from the normal; and a ray bends because it changes speed at a boundary — slowing (air→glass/water) bends it toward the normal, speeding up (glass/water→air) bends it away, while a ray along the normal changes speed but not direction.
learnerActions: Aim one light ray at a flat mirror and vary the angle of the incoming ray; for several angles, measure both the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection FROM the normal (the dashed perpendicular at the point the ray meets the surface), and record the pairs.
State the pattern you find between the two angles in your own words before being told any rule.

Place an object in front of the mirror, trace at least two rays from the same point on it to the mirror and back, then extend the reflected rays backward (as dashed lines) behind the mirror to locate where they appear to meet; mark this virtual image and check that it is upright, the same size as the object, and the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front — and note that it is laterally inverted (left and right swapped).

Swap the mirror for a rectangular (parallel-sided) glass block or water tank. Send the ray in at an angle and describe which way it bends on entering (toward or away from the normal) and which way it bends on leaving the far side.
Set the ray to travel exactly along the normal (0° incidence) and observe whether it changes direction; then tilt it by a small amount and observe again.
If the activity provides a speed indicator, note how the ray's speed changes inside the denser medium and relate that change to whether and which way the ray bends.

If a medium control is available (air → water → glass), switch to an optically denser medium (one where light travels more slowly) and, keeping the same angle of incidence, describe what happens to the size of the bend.
activities.title: Ray bench: discover the reflection law and the refraction bend

feedback: If a learner thinks paper 'breaks the law of reflection', show that at each tiny patch angle in still equals angle out; it is the many differently-tilted patches that scatter the rays.
If a learner cannot explain why a mirror images, point back to the parallel rays staying parallel so the eye can reconstruct a single image.

A sorting task can help check that a learner classifies surfaces correctly, but it does not by itself show the ray behaviour — pair it with observing or sketching the parallel-vs-scatter rays so the reason, not just the category, is understood.
activities.intendedInsight: A mirror forms a clear image because its smooth surface keeps reflected rays parallel (specular reflection); a rough surface scatters rays (diffuse reflection) so no image forms — but both obey the law of reflection locally, so the difference is surface smoothness, not a different law.
learnerActions: Shine a bundle of parallel rays at a smooth surface (mirror) and at a rough surface (paper); observe and sketch what happens to the rays in each case.
Note that on the smooth surface the parallel rays stay parallel after reflecting, while on the rough surface they scatter in many directions.
Check that each individual ray still obeys angle in = angle out from the local normal, even on the rough surface — the difference is that the rough surface tilts the normal differently at each point.
Sort a set of surfaces (polished metal, still water, paper, matte wall, etc.) into those that form a clear image and those that do not, and explain your sorting using the parallel-vs-scatter idea.
activities.title: Why a mirror images but paper does not: specular vs diffuse

feedback: Correct full response: bends toward the normal on entry (slowing, air→glass) and away on exit (speeding up, glass→air), with the emergent ray parallel to the incident ray for a parallel-sided block, both bends caused by the speed change at the boundary.

Gap response (bends both boundaries the same way, forgets the exit bend, measures from the surface, or confuses reflection with refraction): rehearse the exit case explicitly and re-establish measuring from the normal.

Partial response (bends toward the normal entering but mishandles the exit, or recites the reflection law without applying the speed-change reason): focus on tracing the speed change at the second boundary.
For the 'glass into air' question, the correct answer is AWAY from the normal; if a learner picks 'toward the normal', revisit which way speed changes on leaving the glass.

If a learner thinks a ray can only reflect OR refract at a surface: a boundary can do both at once — some light reflects (angle in = angle out) while some refracts (passes through and changes direction); these are different behaviours, not alternatives.
activities.intendedInsight: Which way a ray bends depends on whether it speeds up or slows down at that particular boundary — so a single angled ray bends toward the normal entering the glass and away on leaving, emerging parallel to the incident ray for a parallel-sided block; this cannot be answered by one memorised rule applied to both boundaries.
learnerActions: Consider a ray of light that goes from air INTO a glass block, travels through it, and comes back OUT into the air on the far side.
Describe how the ray bends at EACH boundary — going in and coming out — and state whether it bends toward or away from the normal in each case.
Explain WHY it bends at each boundary in terms of the speed change.
Answer a direction question: a ray goes from glass into air — which way does it bend? (Watch the tempting but wrong 'toward the normal' answer.)
Trace the full path of the ray through a rectangular (parallel-sided) air→glass→air block, including the exit bend, and show that the emerging ray is parallel to the incident ray.
activities.title: Two-tier diagnostic: both boundaries of one ray
